title: 2  Intro
text:
2.2 Note on variable denominations
For various reasons, the variable names in the NetLogo model and the ones used in the analysis and plotting code do not always match directly. In general, the variable names in the analysis code are contrained by their usability in R scripting (e.g., no hyphens or special characters besides underscores), while the original variable names are adapted to NetLogo’s conventions (i.e. using hyphens). The parameters inherited by the model from the Coale-Demeny and Peristera-Kostaki models are named after the original parameters in those models (e.g., mu_women), whose meaning might be immediatly less clear than other, more extensive parameter names. Moreover, some variables in the analysis code are derived or transformed versions of the original NetLogo variables (e.g., log_totalIndividuals is the logarithm of totalIndividuals in NetLogo). For example, cdmlt_level in the analysis corresponds to cdmlt-level in NetLogo, and c1_fert corresponds to c1-fert. When interpreting the results, it’s important to keep this mapping in mind to understand which parameters are being referred to in each context.

title: 3  Age-dependent demographic schedules and ecological weights
text:
3.1 Setup
This chapter visualises the age-dependent functions used by the Household Demography model. Its purpose is diagnostic rather than inferential: the plots show the shapes produced by the model equations and make the consequences of changing their parameters easier to inspect.
Three distinct components are considered:
The first two components define event probabilities. The demand and labour functions instead assign relative weights to individuals according to age. None of the illustrative parameter sets below should be interpreted as calibration to a particular historical population.
Code
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(purrr)
library(ggplot2)
library(patchwork)
library(demogR)

FIGURE_DIR <- "plots/equation_visualisation"

dir.create(
  FIGURE_DIR,
  recursive = TRUE,
  showWarnings = FALSE
)

theme_schedule <- function(base_size = 11) {
  theme_classic(base_size = base_size) +
    theme(
      legend.position = "right",
      legend.title = element_text(size = rel(0.9)),
      legend.text = element_text(size = rel(0.82)),
      strip.background = element_blank(),
      strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
      plot.tag = element_text(face = "bold"),
      plot.margin = margin(5.5, 8, 5.5, 5.5)
    )
}

save_plot_set <- function(
  plot,
  filename,
  width,
  height,
  dpi = 600
) {
  path_stem <- file.path(FIGURE_DIR, filename)

  ggsave(
    paste0(path_stem, ".png"),
    plot = plot,
    width = width,
    height = height,
    units = "in",
    dpi = dpi,
    bg = "white"
  )

  ggsave(
    paste0(path_stem, ".pdf"),
    plot = plot,
    width = width,
    height = height,
    units = "in",
    device = grDevices::cairo_pdf,
    bg = "white"
  )

  ggsave(
    paste0(path_stem, ".eps"),
    plot = plot,
    width = width,
    height = height,
    units = "in",
    device = grDevices::cairo_ps,
    onefile = FALSE,
    fallback_resolution = dpi,
    bg = "white"
  )

  invisible(plot)
}
The export helper writes a high-resolution PNG for the notebook, a PDF for inspection, and an EPS file for the manuscript. The EPS output uses standard vector text and lines and contains no embedded title or equation.

title: 3  Age-dependent demographic schedules and ecological weights
text:
3.2 Peristera–Kostaki schedules
The Peristera–Kostaki function is:
\[
f_{\mathrm{PK}}(x)
=
c_1
\exp\left[
-\left(
\frac{x-\mu}{\sigma(x)}
\right)^2
\right],
\qquad
\sigma(x)
=
\begin{cases}
\sigma_1, & x \leq \mu,\\
\sigma_2, & x > \mu.
\end{cases}
\]
Here, (c_1) controls the maximum probability, () the modal age, and (_1) and (_2) the spread before and after the mode. The same functional form is used for fertility and union formation, with separate parameterisations.


Code
pk_probability <- function(
  age,
  c1,
  mu,
  sigma1,
  sigma2
) {
  sigma <- if_else(age <= mu, sigma1, sigma2)

  c1 * exp(
    -((age - mu) / sigma)^2
  )
}

generate_pk_schedule <- function(
  c1,
  mu,
  sigma1,
  sigma2,
  max_age = 100
) {
  tibble(age = 0:max_age) |>
    mutate(
      probability = pk_probability(
        age,
        c1,
        mu,
        sigma1,
        sigma2
      )
    )
}


The vectorised function returns a tidy table rather than growing a vector inside a loop. This makes it easier to generate, combine, and label multiple schedules.


Code
pk_profiles <- tribble(
  ~profile, ~c1, ~mu, ~sigma1, ~sigma2,
  "c1=.33, mu=25, sigma1=6, sigma2=10", 0.33, 25, 6, 10,
  "c1=.45, mu=20, sigma1=2, sigma2=7",  0.45, 20, 2, 7,
  "c1=.28, mu=25, sigma1=4, sigma2=15", 0.28, 25, 4, 15,
  "c1=.30, mu=18, sigma1=2, sigma2=15", 0.30, 18, 2, 15
)

pk_data <- pk_profiles |>
  mutate(
    schedule = pmap(
      list(c1, mu, sigma1, sigma2),
      generate_pk_schedule
    )
  ) |>
  select(profile, schedule) |>
  unnest(schedule)




Code
plot_pk <- ggplot(
  pk_data,
  aes(
    x = age,
    y = probability,
    colour = profile
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 100),
    breaks = seq(0, 100, 20),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 0.5),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Annual event probability",
    colour = NULL
  ) +
  theme_schedule()

plot_pk








Figure 3.1: Illustrative Peristera–Kostaki schedules. The selected profiles show how peak probability, modal age, and the pre- and post-modal spreads alter the timing and shape of annual fertility or union-formation probabilities.





For closer inspection of parameter effects, a one-at-a-time grid is often more informative than adding further curves to the manuscript figure.


Code
pk_reference <- list(
  c1 = 0.33,
  mu = 25,
  sigma1 = 6,
  sigma2 = 10
)

pk_parameter_values <- list(
  c1 = c(0.20, 0.33, 0.45),
  mu = c(18, 25, 32),
  sigma1 = c(2, 6, 10),
  sigma2 = c(5, 10, 15)
)

pk_parameter_effects <- imap_dfr(
  pk_parameter_values,
  function(values, parameter) {
    map_dfr(
      values,
      function(value) {
        pars <- pk_reference
        pars[[parameter]] <- value

        generate_pk_schedule(
          c1 = pars$c1,
          mu = pars$mu,
          sigma1 = pars$sigma1,
          sigma2 = pars$sigma2
        ) |>
          mutate(
            parameter = parameter,
            value = as.character(value)
          )
      }
    )
  }
)

ggplot(
  pk_parameter_effects,
  aes(
    x = age,
    y = probability,
    colour = value
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.75) +
  facet_wrap(
    ~ parameter,
    ncol = 2,
    labeller = as_labeller(
      c(
        c1 = "Peak probability (c1)",
        mu = "Modal age (mu)",
        sigma1 = "Pre-modal spread (sigma1)",
        sigma2 = "Post-modal spread (sigma2)"
      )
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 100),
    breaks = seq(0, 100, 20),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 0.5),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.02))
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Annual event probability",
    colour = "Value"
  ) +
  theme_schedule()








Figure 3.2: One-at-a-time exploration of the four Peristera–Kostaki parameters around a common reference schedule.

3.3 Coale–Demeny mortality schedules
The Coale–Demeny component supplies grouped probabilities of dying for four regional model families, two sexes, and 25 mortality levels. The model workflow converts these grouped schedules to annual lookup vectors with the same interpolation used when producing the NetLogo input tables.


Code
read_cd_schedule <- function(
  region = "w",
  sex = "F",
  level = 8,
  table_directory = "../demoTables",
  max_age = 100
) {
  if (!region %in% c("w", "e", "s", "n")) {
    stop("region must be one of: w, e, s, n.")
  }

  if (!sex %in% c("F", "M")) {
    stop("sex must be F or M.")
  }

  if (!level %in% 1:25) {
    stop("level must be between 1 and 25.")
  }

  mortality_table <- read.table(
    file.path(
      table_directory,
      paste0("cdmlt", region, sex, ".txt")
    ),
    header = TRUE,
    check.names = FALSE
  )

  data.frame(
    region = region,
    sex = sex,
    level = level,
    age = mortality_table$age,
    probability =
      mortality_table[[as.character(level)]]
  ) |>
    dplyr::filter(age <= max_age)
}


The interpolation helper intentionally reproduces the lookup construction used by the model workflow. Its purpose here is visual consistency with the probabilities imported by NetLogo, rather than reconstruction of an alternative continuous mortality model.
For the manuscript figure, a single regional family and sex are held constant while mortality level varies. This produces a more legible comparison than changing region, sex, and level simultaneously.


Code

cd_data <- cd_levels |>

      list(region, sex, level),
      read_cd_schedule
    )
  ) |>
  select(schedule) |>
  unnest(schedule) |>
  mutate(
    level_label = factor(
      paste("Level", level),
      levels = paste("Level", c(3, 8, 25))
    )
  )

title: 3  Age-dependent demographic schedules and ecological weights
text:
3.5 Age-weighted demand and labour
Versions v1.2.1 and v1.4.1 replace head count with age-weighted subsistence demand. Versions v1.2.2 and v1.4.2 add an age-weighted labour contribution. Both functions equal one between the lower and upper adult-equivalent breakpoints, (x_m=15) and (x_s=45), but use different exponents outside that interval:
\[
w(x)=
\begin{cases}
\left(\dfrac{x}{x_m}\right)^{a}, & x<x_m,\\
1, & x_m\leq x\leq x_s,\\
\left(\dfrac{x_s}{x}\right)^{b}, & x>x_s.
\end{cases}
\]
For demand, (a=1.2) and (b=2). For labour, (a=b=10). These functions are schematic assumptions rather than calibrated physiological or economic schedules.


Code
age_weight <- function(
  age,
  lower_age = 15,
  upper_age = 45,
  young_exponent,
  old_exponent
) {
  case_when(
    age < lower_age ~
      (age / lower_age)^young_exponent,

    age > upper_age ~
      (upper_age / age)^old_exponent,

    TRUE ~ 1
  )
}

age_weights <- tibble(age = 0:100) |>
  transmute(
    age,
    `Subsistence demand` = age_weight(
      age,
      young_exponent = 1.2,
      old_exponent = 2
    ),
    `Labour contribution` = age_weight(
      age,
      young_exponent = 10,
      old_exponent = 10
    )
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    -age,
    names_to = "weighting",
    values_to = "weight"
  )




Code
plot_age_weights <- ggplot(
  age_weights,
  aes(
    x = age,
    y = weight,
    colour = weighting,
    linetype = weighting
  )
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.85) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 100),
    breaks = c(0, 15, 45, 60, 80, 100),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1.05),
    breaks = seq(0, 1, 0.2),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Relative adult-equivalent weight",
    colour = NULL,
    linetype = NULL
  ) +
  theme_schedule() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

plot_age_weights

save_plot_set(
  plot_age_weights,
  filename = "age_weighted_demand_and_labour",
  width = 7.2,
  height = 3.8
)








Figure 3.7: Age-dependent adult-equivalent weights used for subsistence demand and labour availability. Both functions equal one between ages 15 and 45, while labour contribution declines much more steeply outside this interval.





Overlaying the two functions makes their modelling distinction clearer than presenting them as isolated diagrams. Demand changes gradually across childhood and later life, whereas labour is concentrated within the central adult-age interval.

title: 3  Age-dependent demographic schedules and ecological weights
text:
3.6 Reproducibility notes

The Peristera–Kostaki implementation is shared by fertility and union formation, but each process and sex can use a separate parameter set.
The Coale–Demeny code uses demogR version 0.6.0, the version used to generate the NetLogo lookup tables.
The mortality plots visualise the baseline annual probabilities before any density-dependent increment is added.
The demand and labour functions are deterministic model assumptions. Their role is to make population composition consequential for total demand and effective capacity, not to reproduce a measured universal age profile.
Plot labels and captions use the terminology adopted in the manuscript: subsistence demand, labour contribution, nominal environmental capacity, and labour-adjusted effective capacity.

4.2 Experiment design
Sobol sampling is used to generate a diverse set of parameter combinations across the defined parameter space. This allows us to explore how different parameter configurations affect the model’s outcomes and to identify which parameters are most influential in driving population survival or extinction. The actual sampling was done with generate_sobol.R script, which generates a sample with 2000 parameter combinations across the parameter ranges defined in parameter_ranges.R. These were generated previously with library/generate_sobol.R.

The generated parameter combinations were then used to run simulations in NetLogo’s Behaviour Space, for each combination of residence-rule (“matrilineal-matrilocal” and “patrilineal-patrilocal”) and coale-demeny-region (“north”, “south”, “east”, and “west”), varying the SEED parameter (n = 3) to introduce stochasticity, for a total of 48,000 simulations. Moreover, all runs assume a fixed maturity-age of 15 years old. Note that this constant determines a conservative age solely for social maturity, used as a criterion for household viability, while union-formation and reproductive maturity are regulated probabilistically through the Peristera-Kostaki parameters in the fertility and nuptiality submodels.

text:
4.3 Data loading and preprocessing
Load simulation end states generated with the Sobol-sampled parameter combinations and sampled trajectories datasets. Preprocess datasets to adapt from NetLogo’s specific format and categorise end states and trajectories.


Code
growth_threshold = 5000 # endstates with population equal or higher than this are considered "Growth" cases




Code
endstates <- load_endstates(MODEL_VERSION) |>
  preprocess_simdata(
    model_version = MODEL_VERSION,
    growth_threshold = growth_threshold
  )




Code
sampled_trajectories <- load_trajectories(MODEL_VERSION) |>
  preprocess_simdata(
     model_version = MODEL_VERSION,
     full_trajectory = TRUE
     )
sampled_trajectories_symmetric <- load_trajectories(MODEL_VERSION, suffix = "symmetric") |>
  preprocess_simdata(
     model_version = MODEL_VERSION,
     full_trajectory = TRUE
     )
sampled_trajectories_cdmlt_level <- load_trajectories(MODEL_VERSION, suffix = "cdmlt-level") |>
  preprocess_simdata(
     model_version = MODEL_VERSION,
     full_trajectory = TRUE
     )
sampled_trajectories_c1_fert <- load_trajectories(MODEL_VERSION, suffix = "c1-fert") |>
  preprocess_simdata(
     model_version = MODEL_VERSION,
     full_trajectory = TRUE
     )


In this and all following versions, a classification is made according to whether populations get extinct, survive and/or grow within the maximum number of simulation steps (max-iterations), which is stored in the variable named survival.

4.3.1 Surviving population structure


Code
group_vars = c(
  "survival",
  "residence_rule",
  "coale_demeny_region",
  "mortality_regime",
  "fertility_intensity",
  "fertility_timing",
  "fertility_spread_pre_peak",
  "fertility_spread_post_peak",
  "union_timing_women",
  "union_timing_men",
  "union_intensity_women",
  "union_intensity_men",
  "union_spread_pre_peak_women",
  "union_spread_pre_peak_men",
  "union_spread_post_peak_women",
  "union_spread_post_peak_men"
)

age_structures <- endstates |>

  filter(
    survival != "Extinction"
  ) |>
  
  characterise_mort_fert_nupt_regimes() |>

  prepare_age_structure(
    age_breaks = seq(0, 100, 5),
    normalize = TRUE,
    group_vars = group_vars
  )

age_structure_indicators <- age_structures |>
  compute_age_structure_indicators(group_vars = group_vars)

endstates <- endstates |>
  left_join(
    age_structure_indicators |>
      select(
        run_unique_id,
        median_age,
        youth_share,
        elderly_share,
        dependency_ratio
      ),
    by = "run_unique_id"
  )


Age structures of surviving populations are prepared by categorising them according to the same grouping variables used in the sensitivity analysis, including categorical parameters (i.e., residence_rule, coale_demeny_region) and parameters converted into binary categories based on their median value, exclusively those regulating demographic probabilites (e.g., mortality_regime, fertility_intensity, etc.).
Furthermore, this selection includes the categorical variable survival that distinguishes between populations that became extinct, persisted without reaching the maximum population size, and reached the maximum population size. This allows us to compare the age structures of surviving populations across different demographic regimes and residence systems, and to identify patterns or differences associated with population persistence or growth.
Moreover, a set of indicators is computed for each age structure, including median age, dependency ratios, and measures of age-structure irregularity, which can provide further insights into the demographic characteristics of surviving populations and how they relate to different parameter regimes and residence systems. These indicators can help identify specific features of the age structure associated with population persistence or growth, and understand how different demographic regimes and residence systems may influence the age structure of surviving populations. Namely, the indicators computed include:

median_age: the age that divides the population into two halves, with 50% of the population being younger and 50% being older.

youth_share: the ratio of the population aged 0-14 to the population aged 15-64, which indicates the proportion of dependents in the population.

reproductive_share: the ratio of the population aged 15-64 to the population aged 65 and over, which indicates the proportion of reproductive-age individuals in the population.

elderly_share: the ratio of the population aged 65 and over to the population aged 15-64, which indicates the proportion of elderly dependents in the population.

total_dependency_ratio: the ratio of the population aged 0-14 and 65 and over to the population aged 15-64, which indicates the overall proportion of dependent individuals in the population.

4.4 Overview of end states and dynamics

4.4.1 Population persistence
We start with an overview of end states across residence rules and the categorical “regions” of the Coale-Demeny model (coale-demeny-region), which are the two categorical parameters explored outside the Sobol sampling. The histogram shows the distribution of final population sizes for each residence rule, with different colours indicating whether the population became extinct or survived. The vertical line represents the maximum population size defined in the model, which helps visually assess how many simulations reached or exceeded this threshold. The x-axis can be set to a logarithmic scale to better visualise differences in population sizes among those that survived.


Code
log_max_population <- max(endstates$log_totalIndividuals)

endstates_distrib_size_plot <- endstates |>
  plot_endstate_variable_distribution(
    main_var = "log_totalIndividuals",
    fill_var = "survival",
    facet_var = c("coale_demeny_region", "residence_rule"),
    bins = 40,
    x_axis_label = "Final population size",
    y_axis_label = "Simulation count",
    threshold_values = log_max_population,
    thresholds_linetype = 2,
    x_axis_log10 = TRUE,
    x_max = log_max_population,
    y_axis_log10 = TRUE
  )
endstates_distrib_size_plot





Distribution of final population sizes across residence rules and Coale-Demeny regions.




Across the explored parameter space, non-extinction outcomes are more common than extinction, and most surviving populations reach the imposed max_population threshold. Persistence below this threshold is comparatively uncommon. This reflects the density-independent character of v1.1: once demographic replacement is sufficient to avoid extinction, there is no endogenous mechanism limiting subsequent population growth.


Code
outcome_prop_plot <- endstates |>
  plot_category_proportion_stacked(
    x_var = "residence_rule",
    fill_var = "survival",
    facet_var = "coale_demeny_region",
    facet_ncol = 2,
    facet_scales = "fixed",
    y_axis_label = "Share of simulations"
  )
outcome_prop_plot





Proportion of simulations across survival category, residence rules and Coale-Demeny regions.






Code
outcome_prop_plot_noextinction <- endstates |>
  filter(survival != "Extinction") |>
  plot_category_proportion_stacked(
    x_var = "residence_rule",
    fill_var = "survival",
    facet_var = "coale_demeny_region",
    facet_ncol = 2,
    facet_scales = "fixed",
    y_axis_label = "Share of simulations"
  )
outcome_prop_plot_noextinction





Proportion of surviving simulations across residence rules and Coale-Demeny regions.




Differences associated with residence_rule and coale_demeny_region are small at this aggregate level. The patrilocal-patrilineal rule produces 15,136 surviving runs, compared with 15,061 under the matrilocal-matrilineal rule, a negligible difference relative to the total number of simulations. The broad Sobol exploration therefore provides little evidence that either residence system is intrinsically more conducive to survival; any stronger contrasts observed in individual trajectory experiments should instead be interpreted as conditional on the particular demographic configuration examined.


4.4.2 Temporal trajectories
The parameter configuration use to generate the trajectories is the same across residence rules, except for the residence_rule parameter itself. This allows us to directly compare the population dynamics under different residence systems while controlling for other factors. The configuration used for this was:

Making the male and female nuptiality schedules symmetric substantially reduces the difference between the two residence systems: both now display very similar growth trajectories and reach the population ceiling over approximately the same time scale. The slower patrilocal-patrilineal growth in the preceding experiment therefore appears to arise largely from the interaction between residence rules and the sex-asymmetric nuptiality schedules, rather than from residence organisation alone. Some residual variation remains because residence rules still determine which partners remain within, enter, or leave the simulated population.


4.4.3 Household composition


Code
household_structure_plot <- endstates |> 
  plot_household_structure_faceted_fixed(
    color_var = "max_couple_count_distribution_max",
    point_alpha = 0.5,
    facet_var = "residence_rule",
    facet_ncol = 2,
    facet_scales = "fixed",
    xy_log10 = TRUE,
    x_axis_label = "number of households",
    y_axis_label = "number of individuals",
    color_label = "Max. couple count allowed in a household\n(parametric maximum)",
    legend_position = "bottom"
  )
household_structure_plot









Final population size and household number are strongly related under both residence systems, confirming that household formation broadly tracks population expansion. The relationship is nevertheless not perfectly proportional: the fitted log-log relationships explain about 71% of the variation under matrilocal-matrilineal residence and 79% under patrilocal-patrilineal residence, while the mean household sizes are similar overall (approximately 7.8 and 8.0 individuals, respectively).

  sampled_trajectories |>
  group_by(residence_rule) |>
  mutate(
    household_structure_ratio = (totalIndividuals / totalHouseholds)
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  plot_trajectories(

    trajectory_id = "run_unique_id",

  )

  sampled_trajectories |>
  group_by(residence_rule) |>
  mutate(
    household_structure_ratio = if_else(totalHouseholds == 0, 0, (totalIndividuals / totalHouseholds)),
    # Find the absolute peak value within the entire residence rule
    global_max = max(household_structure_ratio, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  group_by(residence_rule, run_number) |>
  mutate(
    # Check if this specific run contains that global peak value
    selected_trajectory = any(household_structure_ratio == global_max)
  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  plot_trajectories(
    y_var = "household_structure_ratio",
    trajectory_id = "run_unique_id",
    line_alpha = 0.035,
    median_alpha = 0.8,
    median_linewidth = 1,

    group_var = NULL,
    facet_var = "residence_rule",
    facet_ncol = 2,
    facet_scales = "free_x",
    y_threshold_var = NULL
  ) +
  # Add the highlighted layer on top
  geom_line(
    data = \(df) filter(df, selected_trajectory == TRUE),
    aes(
      x = step, 
      y = household_structure_ratio,
      group = run_number
    ),
    color = "red",
    linewidth = 1,
    alpha = 1
  )

The trajectory experiment reveals the more informative difference. Both residence systems undergo an early decline followed by a temporary increase in mean household size before converging towards broadly similar late-run values. The transient is larger and more variable under patrilocal-patrilineal residence, reaching higher household sizes in some stochastic realisations, but it does not constitute a sustained increase. Residence organisation therefore appears to affect the transient balance between household growth and fission more strongly than the eventual mean household size.


4.4.4 Age structure

4.4.4.1 Survival categories

The distinction between Persistence and Growth is associated with a very large difference in age structure. Persistent populations have a mean median age of 29.6 years, compared with 18.6 years among populations reaching max_population, and their juvenile representation is correspondingly much lower. Cohen’s (d=1.92) indicates a large separation between the two distributions.
Growth in this density-independent model is therefore associated with strong cohort renewal: rapidly expanding populations accumulate large juvenile cohorts and maintain comparatively young age structures. Populations that remain below the technical population ceiling are substantially older and less juvenile. The contrast should not be interpreted as two alternative demographic equilibria, since v1.1 contains no density-dependent stabilising mechanism; rather, it distinguishes configurations capable of rapid sustained growth from those producing much slower demographic turnover.

Residence rule and Coale-Demeny region introduce only modest variation compared with the much stronger contrast between survival categories. Across surviving populations as a whole, median age differs negligibly between residence systems (Cohen’s (d=0.045)). Regional mortality schedules produce somewhat greater variation, with South generally yielding the oldest and West the youngest age structures, but these differences remain small relative to the Persistence-versus-Growth distinction.

text:
4.5 Sensitivity analysis

4.5.1 Prepare data for sensitivity analysis
Prepare a dataframe out of endstates that contains only predictors (explored parameters) and response variables (survival, log_totalIndividuals, median_age), as well as splitting it according to residence_rule.


Code
response_variables <- c(
  "log_totalIndividuals",
  "survival",
  "median_age"
)

sensitivity_data <- prepare_sensitivity_data_by_residence_rule(
  endstates,
  response_variables,
  parameter_metadata
)




4.5.2 Fitting Random-forest models


Code
rf_models <- load_or_build_rf_models(
  model_version = MODEL_VERSION,
  sensitivity_data = sensitivity_data,
  response_variables = response_variables,
  SEED = 123,
  verbose = FALSE,
  overwrite = REMAKE_RF
)


Random forest models are fitted separately for each residence rule and response variable, using the same set of predictors. The primary response variable, survival, classifies end states as extinction, persistence, or growth, using parameter combinations as categorical outcomes. The more nuanced response variables log_totalIndividuals and median_age are used only after filtering the data to include cases where a population is present at the end state (i.e. survival != "Extinction").
The models are built using a consistent random seed to ensure reproducibility, and the option to overwrite existing models is controlled by the REMAKE_RF flag.


4.5.3 Parameter importance and partial dependence

4.5.3.1 Survival (probability of extinction end state)


Code
rf_survival_importance <- bind_rows(
  
  extract_importance(
    rf_models$survival$matri
  ) |>
    mutate(
      residence_rule = "matrilocal-matrilineal"
    ),
  
  extract_importance(
    rf_models$survival$patri
  ) |>
    mutate(
      residence_rule = "patrilocal-patrilineal"
    )
)

param_color <- parameter_metadata$color[match(rf_survival_importance$parameter, parameter_metadata$parameter)]


Note: associated colours for parameters based on their domain (general, mortality, fertility, nuptiality).


Code
plot_importance(
  rf_survival_importance, 
  param_color = param_color, 
  facet_var = "residence_rule")





Variable importance for the Random Forest models predicting population survival, by residence rule.






Code
importance_dumbbell_plot <- plot_importance_dumbbell(
  rf_survival_importance, 
  groups = "residence_rule", 
  param_color = param_color
  )

importance_dumbbell_plot





Variable importance for the Random Forest models predicting population survival, by residence rule, with a dumbbell plot to directly compare the importance of parameters across residence rules.




Select top parameters in relation to survival:


Code
top_parameters_survival <- rf_survival_importance |>
  group_by(parameter) |>
  summarise(
    mean_importance =
      mean(MeanDecreaseGini)
  ) |>
  slice_max(
    mean_importance,
    n = 10
  ) |>
  pull(parameter)


For each top parameter, calculate PDs for the corresponding RFs using survival as response variable and no population (“Extinction”) as response class. Plot each PD result with log_totalIndividuals and per residence_rule.


Code
pd_survival <- load_or_build_pd_results(
  model_version = MODEL_VERSION,
  overwrite = REMAKE_DP, # set REMAKE_DP = TRUE (first code chunk) to overwrite any previous results
  sensitivity_data,
  rf_models,
  parameters = top_parameters_survival,
  response_variable = "survival",
  response_class = "Extinction" # used only with `survival` as response variable
)




Code
param_pd_plots <- plot_parameter_dependence_composite(
  sensitivity_data,
  pd_survival,
  top_parameters_survival,
  response_variable = "log_totalIndividuals",
  pd_label = "P(Extinction)",
  ncol = 2,
  plot_title_margin_bottom = -5
)




Code
plotName = paste0("plots/v11_survival_param_pd.png")

knitr::include_graphics(plotName)





Partial dependence plots for the top parameters influencing population survival, by residence rule.




Population survival in the v1.1 simulations is dominated by fertility intensity. c1_fert has by far the greatest random-forest importance under both residence rules, and its partial dependence shows a steep decline in extinction probability as fertility rises from very low to moderate values. Above this transition, additional increases continue to improve survival more gradually.
A second group of influential parameters describes reproductive scheduling and union formation. Later female union timing (mu_women) increases extinction probability, whereas broader post-peak fertility (sigma2_fert), broader pre-peak female nuptiality (sigma1_women), and greater female union intensity (c1_women) generally reduce it. Mortality intensity (cdmlt_level) remains directionally important, with higher Coale-Demeny levels reducing extinction, but it is substantially less influential than fertility intensity in the exploration and its partial dependence is comparatively gradual rather than threshold-like.
The clearest residence-dependent differences occur among nuptiality parameters. Parameters governing women tend to carry more importance under matrilocal-matrilineal residence, whereas several male nuptiality parameters become more influential under patrilocal-patrilineal residence. This is consistent with the model’s residence mechanism: the demographic consequences of union formation depend on which partner remains within the population and which is drawn from or returned to the external pool.

knitr::include_graphics(plotName)





Partial dependence plots for the top parameters influencing population size, by residence rule.




Conditional on survival, fertility intensity remains the clearest predictor of final population size. c1_fert dominates the importance ranking under both residence rules, while several nuptiality parameters (c1_women, sigma1_women, mu_women, and male counterparts) and mortality intensity contribute at substantially lower levels. The corresponding partial dependence is strongest for fertility intensity: increasing c1_fert rapidly shifts surviving runs towards the imposed population ceiling, whereas the marginal responses to most other parameters are comparatively small.
Final population size in v1.1 should therefore be interpreted cautiously. Because successful expanding populations are terminated at max_population, much of the variation among high-growth configurations is censored at the same endpoint. The response distinguishes configurations that remain relatively small from those that reach the simulation ceiling more effectively than it measures an unconstrained long-term population size.
Differences between residence rules are parameter-specific rather than evidence of uniformly greater demographic responsiveness under one residence system. The results therefore do not support a general claim that matrilocal-matrilineal populations are more sensitive to fertility and mortality variation.

Partial dependence plots for the top parameters influencing median age, by residence rule.




Median age is governed primarily by reproductive turnover rather than mortality intensity. c1_fert is by far the strongest predictor under both residence rules, followed by sigma2_fert; several female and male nuptiality parameters form the next tier. By contrast, cdmlt_level no longer appears among the ten most important predictors of median age.
The partial-dependence relationships are demographically coherent. Higher fertility intensity strongly reduces expected median age by continually replenishing juvenile cohorts, while broader post-peak fertility has a weaker effect in the same direction. Higher union intensities and broader pre-peak union schedules generally also favour younger age structures, whereas later female or male union timing tends to increase median age. The relative importance of male and female nuptiality varies with residence rule, again indicating an interaction between union formation and post-marital residence.
Initial population conditions retain detectable influence, but their importance is secondary to fertility and nuptiality. Thus, results identify reproductive recruitment and its timing, rather than mortality, as the principal determinants of age composition among populations that survive.

High fertility peak intensity regimes produce markedly younger populations, tighter demographic distributions, and reduced ageing. This coincides with what demographic theory predicts: high fertility expands juvenile cohorts, increasing demographic turnover, and lowering overall median age.
The effect is stronger in the matrilocal system, which suggests that fertility intensity may play a more critical role in sustaining population growth and rejuvenation in matrilocal-matrilineal societies compared to patrilocal-patrilineal societies.
Low fertility persistence populations exhibit pronounced upper-age tails, especially under patrilocality, which suggests that low fertility regimes sustain persistence partly through demographic ageing rather than replacement expansion. This is consistent with the partial dependence analysis, where low fertility regimes show a more pronounced effect on population survival in the patri system.
Fertility intensity therefore has a large structural effect under both residence systems, with only a small difference in magnitude between them. The dominant result is not a residence-specific response but the strong demographic rejuvenation associated with higher fertility.

4.5.4.14 Interpretation
Results identify fertility peak intensity as the principal regulator of demographic youthfulness. c1_fert produces by far the largest differences in median age, while post-peak fertility spread (sigma2_fert) and several nuptiality parameters exert smaller secondary effects. Mortality intensity has only a modest effect on age structure among surviving populations.
The strongest structural contrast is instead between demographic outcomes. Populations that reach the growth threshold are much younger and contain substantially larger juvenile cohorts than populations that merely persist, yielding a very large Persistence-versus-Growth effect ((d=1.92)).

This reflects differences in cohort renewal rather than alternative equilibria: v1.1 has no density-dependent mechanism capable of stabilising population size.
Residence organisation has little direct effect on aggregate median age ((d=0.045)), although it modifies the sensitivity of age structure to particular male and female nuptiality parameters. Results therefore point to a hierarchy in which demographic regime and reproductive schedules dominate population structure, while residence rules act mainly as interaction modifiers.

4.8 Discussion notes
The v1.1 results identify fertility intensity as the dominant control on baseline demographic behaviour. c1_fert is by far the strongest predictor of extinction, surviving population size, and median age. Female nuptiality and fertility-schedule shape form an important secondary group of controls, whereas mortality intensity remains directionally important but is much less dominant than indicated by the previous simulation results.
Survival is therefore not governed by a single mortality threshold. Instead, extinction emerges from the combined capacity of the demographic system to replace individuals through fertility and union formation. Partial dependence shows a particularly strong nonlinear response to fertility intensity, while female union timing, union intensity, and fertility spread alter the probability of successful replacement more gradually.
Population composition exhibits an even clearer hierarchy. The largest age-structure difference is between persistent and rapidly growing populations, followed by variation in fertility intensity. Residence rule by itself produces almost no shift in aggregate median age, although it changes the importance of sex-specific nuptiality parameters and generates modest differences in household and trajectory dynamics.
Taken together, v1.1 behaves as a density-independent demographic growth system in which fertility and reproductive scheduling determine whether replacement is sufficient and how rapidly populations expand. Kinship organisation modifies these processes but does not override them.

4.8.1 Residence rule
Residence rule has a small aggregate effect on survival in the global exploration. Patrilocal-patrilineal runs in fact produce marginally more non-extinction outcomes than matrilocal-matrilineal runs, but the difference is too small to support a general ranking of demographic resilience.
Residence organisation matters more through interactions with other mechanisms. In targeted trajectories, sex-asymmetric nuptiality can generate differences in growth tempo, and the random-forest analyses show that female nuptiality parameters tend to become more influential under matrilocal-matrilineal residence whereas male parameters are emphasised under patrilocal-patrilineal residence. Residence rule therefore acts mainly as a modifier of union formation, migration, and household organisation rather than as an independent determinant of survival.


4.8.2 Other parameters
Parameters describing initial household configuration and kinship restrictions generally have much lower importance than fertility and nuptiality variables. Some retain detectable effects, particularly on surviving population size or median age, but none approaches the influence of fertility intensity.
coale_demeny_region also produces relatively small aggregate differences. Regional mortality schedules generate modest variation in end-state survival and age structure, but the present experiments do not isolate which age- or sex-specific components of the regional life tables are responsible. Any mechanistic interpretation of these regional contrasts would therefore require a more targeted decomposition of the Coale-Demeny schedules.


4.8.3 Variability of population structure
Results reveal selective rather than general structural robustness. Age structure is remarkably insensitive to residence rule and only modestly affected by Coale-Demeny region, but it changes strongly with demographic growth regime and fertility intensity. Populations reaching the growth threshold are much younger than persistent populations, and high-fertility regimes substantially increase juvenile representation.
This distinction is important when considering model simplification. Aggregate models that omit age and household structure may reproduce broad changes in total population size when social organisation is not central to the research question. They would, however, miss substantial changes in demographic composition associated with fertility and growth tempo, as well as the residence-dependent interaction of male and female nuptiality. The usefulness of a simpler formulation therefore depends on whether the target phenomenon concerns population abundance alone or the composition and organisation through which that abundance is generated.
crumbs: 4  Base model (v1.1)

title: 4  Base model (v1.1)
text:
4.9 Chapter conclusion
Version 1.1 establishes a density-independent baseline in which fertility intensity and reproductive scheduling dominate population survival, growth rate, and age composition, while residence organisation primarily modifies nuptiality, household dynamics, and demographic tempo. In the absence of ecological regulation, viable parameter combinations generally produce continued expansion towards the imposed population ceiling, providing the reference behaviour against which the density-dependent model versions can be evaluated.

5.2 Experiment design
Sobol sampling is used to generate a diverse set of parameter combinations across the defined parameter space. This allows us to explore how different parameter configurations affect the model’s outcomes and to identify which parameters are most influential in driving population survival or extinction. The actual sampling was done with generate_sobol.R script, which generates a sample with 2,000 parameter combinations across the parameter ranges defined in parameter_ranges.R. As with v1.1, the generated parameter combinations were then used to run simulations in NetLogo’s Behaviour Space, for each combination of residence-rule (“matrilineal-matrilocal” and “patrilineal-patrilocal”) and coale-demeny-region (“north”, “south”, “east”, and “west”), varying the SEED parameter (n = 3) to introduce stochasticity, for a total of 48,000 simulations. 5.3 Data loading and preprocessing
Load simulation end states generated with the Sobol-sampled parameter combinations and sampled trajectories datasets. Preprocess datasets to adapt from NetLogo’s specific format and categorise end states and trajectories.


Code
overshoot_magnitude_threshold <- 0 # any value over carrying capacity is considered overshooting
burn_in_fraction = 0.5 # the second half of the simulation is considered representative of an equilibrium phase
overshoot_time_threshold <- 0.1 # 10% of time after "burn in" period
oscillatory_threshold <- 0.05 # coefficient of variance of population size after "burn in" period 
stress_threshold <- 0.5 # pressures over this value are considered as population under stress




Code
endstates <- load_endstates(MODEL_VERSION) |>
  preprocess_simdata(
    MODEL_VERSION,
    overshoot_magnitude_threshold = overshoot_magnitude_threshold
  )




Code
sampled_trajectories <- load_trajectories(MODEL_VERSION) |>
  preprocess_simdata(
     model_version = MODEL_VERSION,
     full_trajectory = TRUE
     ) |>
  compute_density_metrics(
    burn_in_fraction = burn_in_fraction
  ) |>
  classify_regulation_regimes(
    overshoot_magnitude_threshold = overshoot_magnitude_threshold,
    overshoot_time_threshold = overshoot_time_threshold,
    oscillatory_threshold = oscillatory_threshold,
    stress_threshold = stress_threshold
  )

sampled_trajectories_density_effect_scaling_factor <- load_trajectories(
  MODEL_VERSION, 
  suffix = "density-effect-scaling-factor"
) |>
  preprocess_simdata(
    model_version = MODEL_VERSION,
    full_trajectory = TRUE
  ) |>
  compute_density_metrics(
    burn_in_fraction = burn_in_fraction
  ) |>
  classify_regulation_regimes(
    overshoot_magnitude_threshold = overshoot_magnitude_threshold,
    overshoot_time_threshold = overshoot_time_threshold,
    oscillatory_threshold = oscillatory_threshold,
    stress_threshold = stress_threshold
  )


In this version, survival also exists to differentiate when populations get extinct or survive in qualitatively different states. However, the calculation and interpretation of survival categories are not the same as in v1.1. Before the introduction of the density effect on mortality, “growth” cases were identified as those where births exceeded deaths, producing unbounded exponential growth, which then necessitated imposing max_population to stop simulations. “Persistence” is then defined as all cases where populations are sustained below this limit for a relatively long time (max_iterations).
In v1.2, as in all other subsequent versions with this density component, surviving population trajectories will flatten around a value depending on the interaction of carrying_capacity and the other parameters regulating the density effect on mortality, which may or may not be at a value beyond the technical limit of simulations (i.e. compare max_population with the range explored for carrying_capacity).
Given this difference, and in the sake of retaining a relative version comparability, we now consider as “overshooting” all cases where end state populations are found above the corresponding carrying capacity, and distinguish between “persistence with low pressure” and “persistence with high pressure”, when end state persistent populations are respectively within the first and second half of the carrying capacity. In line with this, a novelty of v1.2 is the creation of pressure (and final_pressure for trajectories) as a measure of population pressure, calculated during preprocess_simdata(), as totalIndividuals / carrying_capacity.
The assessment of pressure allows us to interpret survival categories in terms of whether population persistence occurs under a regulated or high-pressure demographic regime. Unfortunately, any cases of overshooting where carrying capacities are set beyond max_population will be misclassified as “persistence”.
Additionally, as v1.2 qualitatively changes population dynamics, a few metrics are calculated to assess sampled trajectories. These are: peak_population, peak_pressure, equilibrium_pressure_mean and equilibrium_pressure_variance.
Besides collapse (extinction) and overshooting (pass a threshold beyond the carrying capacity), the regulation regimes are classified based on equilibrium_pressure_mean, equilibrium_pressure_variance and final_pressure:

5.3.1 Surviving population structure


Code
group_vars = c(
  "survival",
  "residence_rule",
  "coale_demeny_region",
  "mortality_regime",
  "fertility_intensity",
  "fertility_timing",
  "fertility_spread_pre_peak",
  "fertility_spread_post_peak",
  "union_timing_women",
  "union_timing_men",
  "union_intensity_women",
  "union_intensity_men",
  "union_spread_pre_peak_women",
  "union_spread_pre_peak_men",
  "union_spread_post_peak_women",
  "union_spread_post_peak_men"
)

age_structures <- endstates |>

  filter(
    survival != "Extinction"
  ) |>
  
  characterise_mort_fert_nupt_regimes() |>

  prepare_age_structure(
    age_breaks = seq(0, 100, 5),
    normalize = TRUE,
    group_vars = group_vars
  )

age_structure_indicators <- age_structures |>
  compute_age_structure_indicators(group_vars = group_vars) |>
  # make a binary classification for Cohen's d test
  mutate(
    pressure_regime = ifelse(
      survival == "Persistence\n(low pressure)",
      "Low pressure\nregimes",
      "High pressure\nregimes"
    )
  )

endstates <- endstates |>
  left_join(
    age_structure_indicators |>
      select(
        run_unique_id,
        median_age,
        youth_share,
        elderly_share,
        dependency_ratio
      ),
    by = "run_unique_id"
  )


As in v1.1, age structures of surviving populations are prepared by categorising them according to the same grouping variables used in the sensitivity analysis, as well as the categorical variable survival, which now takes different categories in response to pressure.
Again, a set of indicators is computed that aims to help identify specific features of the age structure associated with parametric conditions. Namely:

median_age: the age that divides the population into two halves, with 50% of the population being younger and 50% being older.

youth_share: the ratio of the population aged 0-14 to the population aged 15-64, which indicates the proportion of dependents in the population.

reproductive_share: the ratio of the population aged 15-64 to the population aged 65 and over, which indicates the proportion of reproductive-age individuals in the population.

elderly_share: the ratio of the population aged 65 and over to the population aged 15-64, which indicates the proportion of elderly dependents in the population.

total_dependency_ratio: the ratio of the population aged 0-14 and 65 and over to the population aged 15-64, which indicates the overall proportion of dependent individuals in the population.

5.4 Overview of end states and dynamics

5.4.1 Population persistence
For consistency and comparison, we provide an overview of end states across residence rules and coale-demeny-region. Remember, the histogram shows the distribution of final population sizes for each residence rule, with different colours indicating whether the population became extinct or survived. The vertical line represents the maximum population size defined in the model, which helps visually assess how many simulations reached or exceeded this threshold. The x-axis can be set to a logarithmic scale to better visualise differences in population sizes among those that survived.


Code
log_max_population <- max(endstates$log_totalIndividuals)

endstates_distrib_size_plot <- endstates |>
  plot_endstate_variable_distribution(
    main_var = "log_totalIndividuals",
    fill_var = "survival",
    facet_var = c("coale_demeny_region", "residence_rule"),
    bins = 40,
    x_axis_label = "Final population size",
    y_axis_label = "Simulation count",
    threshold_values = log_max_population,
    thresholds_linetype = 2,
    x_axis_log10 = TRUE,
    x_max = log_max_population,
    y_axis_log10 = TRUE
  )
endstates_distrib_size_plot





Distribution of final population sizes across residence rules and Coale-Demeny regions.




Population pressure can help us better characterise “persistence” and “growth” in terms of demographic pressure.


Code
endstates_pressure_plot <- endstates |>
  filter(survival != "Extinction") |>
  plot_endstate_variable_distribution(
    main_var = "pressure",
    fill_var = "survival",
    facet_var = c("coale_demeny_region", "residence_rule"),
    bins = 40,
    x_axis_label = "Final population pressure",
    y_axis_label = "Simulation count",
    threshold_values = c(0.5, 1),
    thresholds_linetype = c(2, 1),
    x_axis_log10 = FALSE,
    y_axis_log10 = FALSE
  )
endstates_pressure_plot





Distribution of final population pressure in surviving populations across residence rules and Coale-Demeny regions.




Only a small minority of simulations end above the nominal carrying capacity (n = 1,724, approximately 3.6% of all runs and 5.8% of surviving runs). Most viable parameter configurations therefore settle below the overshooting threshold, although this operational count remains conservative where carrying_capacity exceeds the technical max_population limit.


Code
outcome_prop_plot <- endstates |>
  plot_category_proportion_stacked(
    x_var = "residence_rule",
    fill_var = "survival",
    facet_var = "coale_demeny_region",
    facet_ncol = 2,
    facet_scales = "fixed",
    y_axis_label = "Share of simulations"
  )
outcome_prop_plot





Proportion of simulations across survival category, residence rules and Coale-Demeny regions.




In contrast to the previous interpretation, the introduction of density-dependent mortality does not substantially increase the overall probability of population survival. Approximately 62.3% of v1.2 simulations avoid extinction, very close to the proportion observed in v1.1. The principal effect of density regulation is instead qualitative: parameter configurations that would otherwise support continuing growth are redistributed among low-pressure persistence, high-pressure persistence, and occasional overshooting states.
As in v1.1, differences associated with residence_rule and coale_demeny_region are minor at this aggregate level. Patrilocal-patrilineal populations produce marginally more surviving runs than matrilocal-matrilineal populations (14,988 versus 14,914), but the difference is negligible relative to the size of the experiment. The global exploration therefore provides no basis for ranking either residence system as intrinsically more resilient.

A sample of population trajectories across time steps, faceted by residence rule.




Under this favourable parameter configuration, density-dependent mortality rapidly transforms the initial demographic expansion into a regulated trajectory close to the nominal carrying capacity. Both residence systems converge within the early part of the simulation and subsequently fluctuate around comparatively stable late-run population levels, rather than continuing the unrestricted growth characteristic of v1.1.
Differences between residence systems are modest and concern the position of the regulated state rather than the existence of regulation itself. Matrilocal-matrilineal trajectories tend to maintain somewhat higher population pressure, whereas patrilocal-patrilineal trajectories remain slightly closer to the carrying-capacity threshold. These differences are conditional on the chosen parameter configuration and should not be interpreted as a general residence-rule effect.
Importantly, carrying capacity does not act as a hard ceiling. The equilibrium position depends strongly on density_effect_scaling_factor, so stable populations may remain below, near, or above the nominal capacity. The targeted experiment in Section 5.6 makes this relationship particularly clear.

Mean household size increases during the early demographic expansion and then settles into a relatively stable range under both residence systems, while individual stochastic runs exhibit temporary excursions to larger household sizes. Matrilocal-matrilineal trajectories appear slightly larger on average in this particular configuration, but the difference is modest compared with the within-rule variation. Results therefore provide little evidence for a strong residence-specific divergence in household size in v1.2.

Distribution of mean and CV of population pressure across density regulation regimes and residence rules, for the trajectories sampled.




Under this particular parameter configuration, all sampled trajectories are classified as Overshooting by the current operational criteria. This does not correspond to unstable runaway growth. Instead, the late-run trajectories are highly concentrated around the carrying-capacity threshold and exhibit very low coefficients of variation, indicating stable regulation close to, or slightly above, nominal capacity.
The two residence systems differ mainly in their mean pressure. Matrilocal-matrilineal trajectories cluster slightly above unity, whereas patrilocal-patrilineal trajectories lie very close to the threshold and have slightly lower late-run mean pressure. In both cases, variation through time is far below the threshold used to distinguish stable from oscillatory regimes.
This targeted trajectory sample is therefore atypical of the global Sobol exploration, in which overshooting remains uncommon. Its value lies precisely in showing that an end state classified as Overshooting need not represent explosive or highly oscillatory dynamics: a population can remain stably regulated just above the nominal environmental capacity.

Population pressure is strongly associated with demographic composition. Low-pressure surviving populations are substantially older, with a mean median age of 22.6 years, lower juvenile representation, and lower dependency ratios. High-pressure populations are considerably younger, while overshooting populations display the youngest age structures and the largest relative juvenile cohorts.
The contrast between low- and high-pressure regimes is large (Cohen’s (d=-1.17)), indicating that pressure in v1.2 captures more than relative population abundance. High demographic pressure is closely associated with rapid cohort renewal and the resulting concentration of young dependants, whereas lower-pressure populations maintain slower turnover and more mature age structures.
These older low-pressure populations should not be characterised as demographically unstable on the basis of age structure alone. In the density-regulated model, an older structure can instead reflect a viable population in which recruitment is sufficient for persistence without generating the large juvenile cohorts associated with rapid expansion.

text:
5.5 Sensitivity analysis

5.5.1 Prepare data for sensitivity analysis
Prepare a dataframe out of endstates that contains only predictors (explored parameters) and response variables (pressure, survival, median_age), as well as splitting it according to residence_rule.


Code
response_variables <- c(
  "pressure",
  "survival",
  "median_age"
)

sensitivity_data <- prepare_sensitivity_data_by_residence_rule(
  endstates,
  response_variables,
  parameter_metadata
)




5.5.2 Fitting Random-forest models


Code
rf_models <- load_or_build_rf_models(
  model_version = MODEL_VERSION,
  sensitivity_data = sensitivity_data,
  response_variables = response_variables,
  SEED = 123,
  verbose = FALSE,
  overwrite = REMAKE_RF
)


Random forest models are fitted separately for each residence rule, using the same set of predictors. The response variables include pressure, survival, and median_age, allowing us to assess the importance of predictors for different aspects of population dynamics and structure. Notice that the model built for median_age uses only cases with surviving populations.
While still relevant, the differentiation between extinction and survival or the absolute number of individuals is less relevant in v1.2, given the introduction of the pressure variable, which provides a more nuanced measure of population persistence and growth. Note that survival in this version also reflects the impact of pressure. Therefore, the focus of the sensitivity analysis is on understanding which parameters most strongly influence population pressure and survival outcomes under different residence rules. median_ageis included as before, as it can provide insights into the age structure of surviving populations and how it relates to the parameters explored.
The models are built using a consistent random seed to ensure reproducibility, and the option to overwrite existing models is controlled by the REMAKE_RF flag.


5.5.3 Parameter importance and partial dependence

5.5.3.1 Survival (probability of extinction end state)


Code
rf_survival_importance <- bind_rows(
  
  extract_importance(
    rf_models$survival$matri
  ) |>
    mutate(
      residence_rule = "matrilocal-matrilineal"
    ),

    rf_models$survival$patri
  ) |>

      residence_rule = "patrilocal-patrilineal"
    )

knitr::include_graphics(plotName)





Partial dependence plots for the top parameters influencing population survival, by residence rule.




Population survival in v1.2 is dominated by fertility intensity and the strength of density-dependent mortality. c1_fert remains by far the most important predictor of extinction under both residence rules, while density_effect_scaling_factor occupies a clear second position. This marks the principal departure from v1.1: ecological regulation becomes one of the strongest determinants of demographic viability immediately after it is introduced.
The partial dependence of c1_fert retains the steep nonlinear relationship already observed in the baseline model, with extinction probability falling rapidly as fertility rises through the lower part of its range. In contrast, increasing density_effect_scaling_factor slightly increases extinction probability before reaching a broad plateau. Stronger density regulation therefore suppresses population pressure but can also impose a viability cost through additional mortality.
Nuptiality parameters form the next tier of predictors and retain a residence-specific pattern. Female parameters such as mu_women, sigma1_women, and c1_women are relatively more influential under matrilocal-matrilineal residence, whereas male parameters become more influential under patrilocal-patrilineal residence. Higher post-peak fertility spread (sigma2_fert) also reduces extinction risk.
cdmlt_level remains directionally consistent, with lower baseline mortality improving survival, but it is not among the dominant predictors. carrying_capacity likewise has comparatively little predictive importance within the explored range of 100–10,000.

Partial dependence plots for the top parameters influencing population pressure, by residence rule.




Population pressure reveals a markedly different hierarchy from extinction probability. density_effect_scaling_factor is overwhelmingly the strongest predictor under both residence rules, and its partial dependence is strongly negative: increasing the additional mortality imposed at a given density load progressively lowers the population maintained relative to carrying capacity.
Fertility intensity (c1_fert) is the second most important predictor and has the opposite effect. Higher fertility increases expected population pressure, with most of the increase occurring across low-to-intermediate fertility values before the response approaches a plateau. The same parameter that protects against extinction therefore also drives surviving populations closer to their ecological limit.
The remaining predictors show strong residence-specific asymmetry. Male nuptiality parameters, especially sigma1_men and c1_men, have substantially greater influence under patrilocal-patrilineal residence, whereas female nuptiality parameters are more influential under matrilocal-matrilineal residence. These effects are visible in the partial-dependence curves and are consistent with residence organisation altering which sex-specific union dynamics most strongly affect local demographic recruitment.
cdmlt_level and carrying_capacity have only moderate importance for pressure relative to density scaling and fertility intensity. Higher Coale-Demeny levels tend to increase pressure by reducing baseline mortality, whereas carrying capacity itself produces only a weak marginal response over the range explored.

Fertility intensity is again the dominant predictor of median age among surviving populations. Increasing c1_fert strongly lowers expected median age, reflecting the expansion of juvenile cohorts associated with more rapid demographic renewal.
The next most important predictors are primarily fertility-schedule and nuptiality parameters. 5.5.4.14 Interpretation
Across analyses, age structure is governed primarily by reproductive renewal. Fertility peak intensity is the strongest common predictor, while fertility spread and sex-specific nuptiality parameters provide important secondary controls. Which nuptiality parameters matter most depends on residence organisation, with female schedules receiving greater weight under matrilocal-matrilineal residence and male schedules under patrilocal-patrilineal residence.
Baseline mortality has a substantially weaker direct effect on age composition than previously inferred. Density-related parameters also contribute less to median age than to population pressure or extinction probability. Ecological regulation therefore shapes the demographic regime within which populations persist, whereas fertility and union formation determine much of the internal age structure of those surviving populations.
The strong relationship between pressure and age structure integrates these results: parameter combinations that generate rapid recruitment tend to produce younger populations, larger juvenile cohorts, and higher dependency ratios, which in turn are associated with higher population pressure.

Population trajectories across different density-effect scaling factors, faceted by residence rule.




Introducing even a small positive density effect qualitatively changes the trajectory. Populations cease sustained growth and converge towards stable regulated levels. The location of this equilibrium then declines monotonically as the scaling factor increases: very weak density dependence permits stable populations above nominal carrying capacity, intermediate values regulate populations close to capacity, and stronger values maintain progressively lower population sizes.
No viability threshold or pronounced oscillatory transition is evident within the positive scaling-factor values examined under this favourable demographic configuration. The experiment therefore demonstrates primarily how the scaling factor controls equilibrium population pressure, rather than identifying a collapse threshold.
This result also explains the global sensitivity analysis. Stronger density dependence lowers pressure very effectively, but across the broader parameter space the additional mortality it imposes can increase extinction risk. The same mechanism therefore stabilises population abundance while narrowing the set of demographic configurations capable of persistence.
crumbs: 5  Density-dependent model (v1.2)

title: 5  Density-dependent model (v1.2)
text:
5.7 Discussion notes
Version 1.2 introduces the first explicit negative density-dependent feedback into the Household Demography model. Its principal effect is not to increase the overall probability of survival relative to v1.1, which remains almost unchanged, but to transform the dynamics of surviving populations. Unrestricted expansion is replaced by regulated states distributed across a continuum of population pressure.
Fertility peak intensity remains the dominant demographic determinant. c1_fert is the strongest predictor of extinction and median age and the second strongest predictor of population pressure. High fertility simultaneously reduces extinction risk, increases population pressure, and produces younger age structures. These linked effects identify reproductive recruitment as the main demographic force pushing populations toward ecological constraint.
Density-effect strength provides the corresponding ecological control. density_effect_scaling_factor is the second strongest predictor of extinction and overwhelmingly the strongest predictor of population pressure. Increasing it lowers the population maintained relative to carrying capacity, but also modestly raises extinction probability across the broader parameter space. Density regulation therefore introduces a genuine demographic-ecological trade-off: stronger regulation reduces pressure while making otherwise marginal demographic configurations less viable.
In contrast, the nominal carrying_capacity parameter itself has relatively little predictive importance within the range explored. It sets the scale against which density load is measured, but the realised position of the population relative to that limit is determined more strongly by fertility, nuptiality, baseline mortality, and the intensity of the density response.
Age structure provides another expression of this coupling. Low-pressure populations are older and have lower juvenile dependency, whereas high-pressure and overshooting populations are increasingly dominated by younger cohorts. Population pressure therefore reflects demographic turnover as well as abundance: rapid recruitment generates both the population growth that increases pressure and the juvenile dependency associated with young expanding populations.
Residence organisation remains a secondary modifier. Aggregate survival and median age differ only slightly between residence systems, and household scaling is almost identical. Its clearest influence appears instead in the relative importance of sex-specific nuptiality parameters, with female schedules contributing more strongly under matrilocal-matrilineal residence and male schedules under patrilocal-patrilineal residence.
Overall, v1.2 converts the density-independent demographic engine of v1.1 into a regulated demographic-ecological system without replacing its demographic foundations. Fertility determines much of the pressure placed on the system, while density-dependent mortality determines how strongly that pressure is translated back into demographic constraint.
crumbs: 5  Density-dependent model (v1.2)

title: 5  Density-dependent model (v1.2)
text:
5.8 Chapter conclusion
Version 1.2 demonstrates that adding density-dependent mortality fundamentally changes population dynamics without substantially changing the overall frequency of demographic persistence. Viable populations no longer expand indefinitely but converge toward regulated states whose position relative to nominal carrying capacity is controlled primarily by fertility intensity and the strength of density-dependent mortality. c1_fert remains the central demographic driver, while density_effect_scaling_factor emerges as the principal ecological regulator; baseline mortality, carrying capacity, household parameters, and residence rule play more secondary or context-dependent roles. The resulting coupling between demographic recruitment, population pressure, and age structure provides the baseline density-regulated behaviour against which the demand- and labour-weighted versions can be evaluated.

The overall distribution of end states in v1.2.1 remains very similar to that observed in v1.2. Approximately 62.5% of simulations avoid extinction, compared with 62.3% in v1.2, indicating that weighting ecological pressure by age-specific demand has little effect on the overall probability of demographic persistence across the parameter space explored.
The more noticeable difference concerns the distribution of surviving states. Only 1,080 simulations, approximately 2.3% of all runs and 3.6% of surviving runs, end in the Overshooting category, compared with 1,724 in v1.2. Because younger and older individuals can contribute less than one adult-equivalent unit to carrying-capacity demand, a given population headcount can exert less pressure than under the unweighted formulation. Demand weighting therefore reduces the frequency with which populations exceed the nominal capacity in demand terms without substantially altering their probability of survival.
Residence rule and Coale-Demeny region again have only minor aggregate effects. Patrilocal-patrilineal residence produces marginally more surviving simulations than matrilocal-matrilineal residence (15,031 versus 14,962), while overshooting is almost equally rare under both rules (536 versus 544 cases, respectively). These differences are too small to support a general residence-specific ranking of demographic resilience.

  ) |>
  ungroup() |>
  plot_trajectories(
    y_var = "household_structure_ratio",
    trajectory_id = "run_unique_id",
    line_alpha = 0.035,
    median_alpha = 0.8,
    median_linewidth = 1,
    y_axis_log10 = FALSE,
    y_axis_label = "Mean individual count per household",
    group_var = NULL,
    facet_var = "residence_rule",
    facet_ncol = 2,
    facet_scales = "fixed",
    y_threshold_var = NULL
  ) +
  # Add the highlighted layer on top
  geom_line(
    data = \(df) filter(df, selected_trajectory == TRUE),
    aes(
      x = step, 
      y = household_structure_ratio,
      group = run_number
    ),
    color = "red",
    linewidth = 1,
    alpha = 1
  )

Household-level outcomes remain almost unchanged from v1.2. Population size continues to scale closely with household number under both residence systems, and mean household trajectories converge towards similar ranges. Demand weighting therefore modifies the ecological load generated by household members without directly altering the rules governing household formation, fission, or continuity.


6.4.4 Density regulation dynamics

Distribution of mean and CV of population pressure across density regulation regimes and residence rules, for the trajectories sampled.




Under this particular parameter configuration, all sampled trajectories are classified as Overshooting according to the operational regulation criteria. As in the corresponding v1.2 experiment, however, this classification does not describe unstable runaway growth. Late-run pressures remain tightly concentrated near unity and show very low coefficients of variation, indicating stable regulation close to the nominal demand capacity.
Demand weighting changes the interpretation of this regulated state. Pressure now measures total age-weighted carrying-capacity demand relative to environmental capacity rather than headcount relative to capacity. Consequently, a population may contain substantially more individuals than the numerical value of carrying_capacity while remaining regulated close to a pressure of one.
The two residence systems again differ only modestly in their late-run mean pressure. The targeted sample therefore reinforces the broader result that demand weighting changes the demographic meaning of ecological load more than the qualitative form of density regulation itself.

The broad age-structure patterns remain almost unchanged from v1.2. Residence rule has a very small aggregate effect on median age ((d=0.076)), and regional differences are likewise modest. By contrast, the distinction between low- and high-pressure populations remains large under both matrilocal-matrilineal ((d=-1.13)) and patrilocal-patrilineal ((d=-1.26)) residence.
What changes in v1.2.1 is the causal architecture connecting age structure to ecological regulation. Pressure is now calculated from the age-weighted demand generated by the population, so demographic composition contributes directly to the mortality feedback rather than merely covarying with it. Fertility-driven differences in recruitment remain the dominant source of variation.

text:
6.5 Sensitivity analysis

6.5.1 Prepare data for sensitivity analysis
Prepare a dataframe out of endstates that contains only predictors (explored parameters) and response variables (pressure, survival, median_age), as well as splitting it according to residence_rule.


Code
response_variables <- c(
  "pressure",
  "survival",
  "median_age"
)

sensitivity_data <- prepare_sensitivity_data_by_residence_rule(
  endstates,
  response_variables,
  parameter_metadata
)




6.5.2 Fitting Random-forest models


Code
rf_models <- load_or_build_rf_models(
  model_version = MODEL_VERSION,
  sensitivity_data = sensitivity_data,
  response_variables = response_variables,
  SEED = 123,
  verbose = FALSE,
  overwrite = REMAKE_RF
)


Random forest models are fitted separately for each residence rule, using the same set of predictors. The response variables include pressure, survival, and median_age, allowing us to assess the importance of predictors for different aspects of population dynamics and structure. Notice that the model built for median_age uses only cases with surviving populations.
The models are built using a consistent random seed to ensure reproducibility, and the option to overwrite existing models is controlled by the REMAKE_RF flag.


6.5.3 Parameter importance and partial dependence

6.5.3.1 Survival (probability of extinction end state)


Code
rf_survival_importance <- bind_rows(
  
  extract_importance(
    rf_models$survival$matri
  ) |>
    mutate(
      residence_rule = "matrilocal-matrilineal"
    ),
  
  extract_importance(
    rf_models$survival$patri
  ) |>
    mutate(
      residence_rule = "patrilocal-patrilineal"
    )
)

param_color <- parameter_metadata$color[match(rf_survival_importance$parameter, parameter_metadata$parameter)]


Note: associated colours for parameters based on their domain (general, mortality, fertility, nuptiality, density).

  param_color = param_color, 
  facet_var = "residence_rule")

    mean_importance,

plotName = paste0("plots/v121_survival_param_pd.png")

knitr::include_graphics(plotName)





Partial dependence plots for the top parameters influencing population survival, by residence rule.




Population survival in v1.2.1 is governed by essentially the same parameter hierarchy as in v1.2. Fertility peak intensity (c1_fert) remains by far the strongest predictor of extinction, followed by density_effect_scaling_factor. Increasing fertility sharply reduces extinction probability across the lower part of its range, whereas stronger density-dependent mortality slightly increases extinction risk before the response approaches a broad plateau.
Nuptiality parameters form the next tier and retain the same residence-specific asymmetry observed previously. Female union timing, intensity, and pre-peak spread are relatively more important under matrilocal-matrilineal residence, whereas male nuptiality parameters gain importance under patrilocal-patrilineal residence. sigma2_fert also remains an important common predictor.
The introduction of age-weighted demand therefore has little effect on the global determinants of demographic viability. It changes how density load is calculated once a population exists, but extinction remains controlled primarily by reproductive replacement and the mortality cost imposed by density regulation. Baseline mortality (cdmlt_level) and nominal carrying capacity remain secondary within the parameter ranges explored.
