The trajectory experiment shows an initial increase in mean household size followed by prolonged fluctuation around a stable range. Occasional trajectories reach substantially larger household sizes, but these excursions are temporary and are not followed systematically by population collapse. They are better interpreted as stochastic episodes of household aggregation than as indicators of demographic instability.
Differences between residence systems are modest, although the largest transient household-size peaks occur in the matrilocal-matrilineal sample.


10.4.4 Density regulation dynamics

Distribution of mean and CV of population pressure across density regulation regimes and residence rules, for the trajectories sampled.




The targeted trajectories occupy an exceptionally consistent regulatory regime. All sampled runs under both residence systems are classified as Stress-prone, with late-run mean pressures close to the upper part of the persistence range and very low coefficients of variation.
This combination indicates stable regulation under sustained high ecological pressure rather than oscillatory instability. Although the daily population trajectories exhibit visible short-term stochastic fluctuations, these do not translate into large long-run variation in pressure.
Residence rule has little effect on the regulatory regime under this configuration. Matrilocal-matrilineal and patrilocal-patrilineal populations occupy almost the same region of mean-CV space, showing that demand-weighted density dependence can produce highly similar stable equilibria despite differences in household organisation.

10.5 Sensitivity analysis

10.5.1 Prepare data for sensitivity analysis
Prepare a dataframe out of endstates that contains only predictors (explored parameters) and response variables (pressure, survival, median_age), as well as splitting it according to residence_rule.


Code
response_variables <- c(
  "pressure",
  "survival",
  "median_age"
)

sensitivity_data <- prepare_sensitivity_data_by_residence_rule(
  endstates,
  response_variables,
  parameter_metadata
)




10.5.2 Fitting Random-forest models


Code
rf_models <- load_or_build_rf_models(
  model_version = MODEL_VERSION,
  sensitivity_data = sensitivity_data,
  response_variables = response_variables,
  SEED = 123,
  verbose = FALSE,
  overwrite = REMAKE_RF
)


Random forest models are fitted separately for each residence rule, using the same set of predictors. The response variables include pressure, survival, and median_age, allowing us to assess the importance of predictors for different aspects of population dynamics and structure. Notice that the model built for median_age uses only cases with surviving populations.
The models are built using a consistent random seed to ensure reproducibility, and the option to overwrite existing models is controlled by the REMAKE_RF flag.


10.5.3 Parameter importance and partial dependence

10.5.3.1 Survival (probability of extinction end state)


Code
rf_survival_importance <- bind_rows(
  
  extract_importance(
    rf_models$survival$matri
  ) |>
    mutate(
      residence_rule = "matrilocal-matrilineal"
    ),
  
  extract_importance(
    rf_models$survival$patri
  ) |>
    mutate(
      residence_rule = "patrilocal-patrilineal"
    )
)

param_color <- parameter_metadata$color[match(rf_survival_importance$parameter, parameter_metadata$parameter)]


Note: associated colours for parameters based on their domain (general, mortality, fertility, nuptiality).

  param_color = param_color, 
  facet_var = "residence_rule")





Variable importance for the Random Forest models predicting population survival, by residence rule.

    mean_importance =
      mean(MeanDecreaseGini)

    mean_importance,

For each top parameter, calculate PDs for the corresponding RFs using survival as response variable and no population (“Extinction”) as response class. Plot each PD result with survival and per residence_rule.

knitr::include_graphics(plotName)





Partial dependence plots for the top parameters influencing population survival, by residence rule.




Fertility peak intensity (c1_fert) is overwhelmingly the strongest predictor of extinction under both residence systems. Its partial dependence shows a steep decline in extinction probability as fertility rises through the lower part of its range, confirming reproductive replacement as the principal determinant of demographic viability.
Female union-formation parameters, particularly pre-peak spread (sigma1_women) and modal timing (mu_women), form an important secondary tier, together with post-peak fertility spread (sigma2_fert). density_effect_scaling_factor, nominal carrying capacity, female union peak intensity, and baseline mortality contribute at lower but still appreciable levels.
Survival in v1.4.1 is therefore governed primarily by reproductive recruitment and union formation, with ecological regulation providing an additional constraint. Baseline mortality is influential but does not dominate the sensitivity hierarchy.

Partial dependence plots for the top parameters influencing population pressure, by residence rule.




Population pressure is controlled jointly by demographic recruitment and ecological feedback. Fertility peak intensity is the strongest predictor, with higher fertility increasing age-weighted demand relative to carrying capacity. density_effect_scaling_factor follows closely and has the opposite effect: stronger density-dependent mortality lowers the pressure maintained by surviving populations.
Baseline mortality and nominal carrying capacity form the next tier of predictors, while male and female union parameters contribute secondary variation. Higher Coale-Demeny levels generally permit greater pressure by reducing baseline mortality, whereas stronger ecological feedback suppresses it.
Demand weighting adds an important compositional dimension to this response. Pressure is not simply a function of population headcount but of the age-specific consumption demand generated by that population. Fertility and union formation can therefore influence ecological load through both population abundance and demographic composition.

Fertility peak intensity is by far the strongest predictor of median age among surviving populations. Male union peak intensity, post-peak fertility spread, female union peak intensity, male pre-peak union spread, and postpartum amenorrhoea form the principal secondary tier.
Baseline mortality has comparatively little importance for median age, despite its relevance to survival and population pressure. The age composition of surviving populations is therefore determined primarily by reproductive recruitment, union formation, and birth spacing rather than by differences in mortality intensity.
Demand-weighted regulation does not overturn this demographic hierarchy. Instead, it links the age structure produced by these mechanisms more directly to ecological pressure by assigning different carrying-capacity demands to individuals of different ages.

10.5.4.15 Interpretation
Fertility peak intensity remains the principal determinant of age structure in v1.4.1. Fertility spread, male union timing and pre-peak union spread, and union peak intensities provide secondary influences, while postpartum amenorrhoea contributes a smaller but consistent ageing effect through birth spacing.
Baseline mortality has virtually no direct association with median age among surviving populations. The different response variables therefore reveal a useful division of demographic roles: fertility and union formation primarily shape cohort composition, whereas mortality and ecological feedback are more consequential for survival and population pressure.
Demand weighting adds a direct connection between these demographic structures and ecological load, because the age composition generated by reproductive processes now determines the total carrying-capacity demand exerted by the population.

title: 10  Demand-weighted density dependent model with daily iteration (v1.4.1)
text:
10.6 Discussion notes
Version 1.4.1 combines daily demographic scheduling with age-weighted ecological demand. Population pressure is therefore determined not simply by the number of individuals but by the demand generated by their age composition, while births, deaths, union formation, gestation, and postpartum amenorrhoea unfold through the daily demographic cycle.
The model produces a broad range of end states, dominated by extinction and low-pressure persistence, with high-pressure persistence less frequent and overshooting rare. Under the favourable reference configuration, however, both residence systems converge on highly stable Stress-prone trajectories. Demand-weighted density dependence can therefore maintain populations close to ecological constraint without producing substantial long-run oscillation.
Fertility peak intensity remains the dominant demographic control. It strongly determines survival, population pressure, and median age. Density-effect strength provides the principal ecological counterweight, reducing realised pressure as feedback intensifies. Baseline mortality contributes to survival and pressure but has little direct effect on age structure among survivors.
Age weighting makes demographic composition ecologically consequential. The same reproductive mechanisms that determine juvenile recruitment and median age also alter total carrying-capacity demand, creating a direct pathway from reproductive schedules to ecological pressure.
Residence rule remains secondary at the aggregate level. Patrilocal-patrilineal populations show a small survival advantage in the global exploration, while matrilocal-matrilineal populations are slightly older on average. In the targeted trajectory experiment, however, both residence systems occupy virtually identical Stress-prone regimes. Residence effects are therefore conditional and are expressed more clearly through particular sex-specific union parameters than through a general difference in resilience.
The comparison with the yearly demand-weighted formulation indicates that temporal resolution changes the quantitative expression of demographic turnover and pressure, but the daily model should not be regarded simply as a smoother version of the yearly one. Explicit reproductive delays and event timing alter the pathway through which demographic demand accumulates, even though the principal fertility-driven architecture remains recognisable.
crumbs: 10  Demand-weighted density dependent model with daily iteration (v1.4.1)

title: 10  Demand-weighted density dependent model with daily iteration (v1.4.1)
text:
10.7 Chapter conclusion
Version 1.4.1 establishes the daily demand-weighted density-regulated formulation of the Household Demography model. Fertility peak intensity remains the dominant demographic driver, while density-effect strength provides the principal ecological regulation of population pressure. Age-weighted demand adds an explicit compositional dimension by making ecological load depend on who comprises the population rather than on headcount alone.
Surviving populations are usually maintained below the nominal demand threshold, although favourable parameter combinations can sustain stable high-pressure states for centuries. Age structure remains governed primarily by fertility, union formation, and birth spacing, whereas baseline mortality and density regulation act more strongly on viability and ecological pressure.
The model therefore provides the appropriate daily demand-side foundation for v1.4.2, where productive labour is added to the supply side and effective carrying capacity becomes endogenous to demographic composition.

11.2 Experiment design
As version v1.4.2 introduces a new parameter, labour_demand_per_capita, an additional batch of Sobol sampled values is generated. As in v1.4.1, this model does require constants used to determine the correspondence between age and the adult-equivalent unit (i.e., 15, 45, and the exponent 10, which determines a steeper decline compared with the function for demand; see get-labour-at-age).
As one of the daily iteration versions, only 512 configurations of the original Sobol exploration sample ((n=2,000)) was used to obtain sufficiently-robust results. The end states data set then contains 12,288 runs (512 configurations × 2 residence rules × 4 Coale-Demeny regions × 3 replicates).

  plot_category_proportion_stacked(
    x_var = "residence_rule",

outcome_prop_plot





Proportion of simulations across survival category, residence rules and Coale-Demeny regions.




The addition of labour-dependent effective carrying capacity imposes a strong viability constraint across the explored parameter space. Extinction is by far the most frequent end state under both residence rules and across all Coale-Demeny regions, while only a comparatively small subset of parameter configurations supports long-term persistence.
Among surviving populations, both low- and high-pressure states occur, while overshooting is uncommon. In v1.4.2, these categories integrate both sides of the demographic-ecological balance: pressure expresses age-weighted carrying-capacity demand relative to the effective capacity that can actually be realised through available labour. A population may therefore experience high pressure either because demographic demand is large, because productive labour constrains effective capacity, or through both processes simultaneously.
Residence rule and Coale-Demeny region produce comparatively modest differences in the aggregate distribution of outcomes. The dominant pattern is the strong restriction of the viable parameter space produced by the interaction between demographic demand and labour-mediated productive capacity.

Under the selected reference configuration, both residence systems remain viable throughout the simulation horizon and rapidly converge towards bounded population levels. Individual stochastic trajectories fluctuate around these long-run levels, but there is no evidence of systematic decline or delayed collapse in either residence system.
The realised population sizes are also strikingly similar between residence rules. Because regulation is based on age-weighted demand relative to labour-mediated effective carrying capacity, the numerical relationship between headcount and nominal carrying_capacity is not itself sufficient to diagnose ecological pressure. The relevant quantity is the demand generated by the population relative to the capacity that its available labour can actually realise.
These trajectories therefore represent a favourable demographic configuration in which productive labour remains sufficient to support stable long-term regulation.

The labour ratio of a sample of population trajectories across time steps, faceted by residence rule.




The global end-state distributions show that labour limitation remains active among populations that survive. Labour ratios span values both below and above unity, and substantial overlap occurs among low-pressure persistence, high-pressure persistence, and overshooting outcomes. Survival therefore does not require populations to maintain enough labour to realise the full nominal carrying capacity.
When labour supply is insufficient, effective carrying capacity falls below the nominal environmental maximum. Because population pressure is calculated as age-weighted demand divided by this effective capacity, a reduction in productive capacity directly raises pressure even if demographic demand remains unchanged. Labour limitation can consequently intensify density-dependent mortality without requiring an increase in population abundance.
At the same time, populations can persist while effective capacity remains partially constrained. Labour limitation therefore does not operate simply as a binary sufficiency test: it continuously changes the ecological denominator against which demographic demand is evaluated.
The reference trajectory ensemble represents a relatively labour-sufficient part of this behavioural space. Its labour ratios remain above unity through most of the simulation, allowing laboured_share to remain close to one and effective carrying capacity to approach its nominal environmental maximum. Across the global exploration, however, viable states also occur under sustained partial labour limitation.

All sampled trajectories are classified as Stress-prone under the reference configuration. Their late-run mean pressures lie within a narrow high-pressure range, while coefficients of variation remain extremely low. The daily trajectories therefore represent stable regulation under sustained demographic-ecological pressure rather than oscillatory or unstable behaviour.
Residence rule has little effect on this regulatory regime. Matrilocal-matrilineal and patrilocal-patrilineal trajectories occupy almost the same region of mean-pressure and variability space, reinforcing the similarity already visible in their population trajectories.
In v1.4.2, population pressure integrates both demographic demand and productive supply. The numerator is the age-weighted carrying-capacity demand generated by the population, while the denominator is the effective carrying capacity realised through age-dependent labour availability. Pressure can therefore increase because demand rises, because effective capacity contracts, or because both processes occur together.
This gives the pressure metric its fullest demographic interpretation in the model series. It no longer represents abundance alone or even age-weighted consumption alone, but the realised balance between what the population demands and what its demographic composition enables it to produce.

Residence rule produces a small but consistent difference in age structure. Matrilocal-matrilineal populations are older and contain smaller juvenile shares across all Coale-Demeny regions, yielding an overall effect of (d=0.31). Regional mortality families introduce comparatively modest variation within each residence system.

text:
11.5 Sensitivity analysis

11.5.1 Prepare data for sensitivity analysis
Prepare a dataframe out of endstates that contains only predictors (explored parameters) and response variables (pressure, survival, median_age), as well as splitting it according to residence_rule.


Code
response_variables <- c(
  "pressure",
  "survival",
  "median_age",
  "log_carrying_capacity_effective"
)

sensitivity_data <- prepare_sensitivity_data_by_residence_rule(
  endstates,
  response_variables,
  parameter_metadata
)




11.5.2 Fitting Random-forest models


Code
rf_models <- load_or_build_rf_models(
  model_version = MODEL_VERSION,
  sensitivity_data = sensitivity_data,
  response_variables = response_variables,
  SEED = 123,
  verbose = FALSE,
  overwrite = REMAKE_RF
)


Random forest models are fitted separately for each residence rule, using the same set of predictors. The response variables include pressure, survival, median_age, and log_carrying_capacity_effective allowing us to assess the importance of predictors for different aspects of population dynamics and structure. Notice that the model built for median_age and log_carrying_capacity_effective uses only cases with surviving populations.
The models are built using a consistent random seed to ensure reproducibility, and the option to overwrite existing models is controlled by the REMAKE_RF flag.


11.5.3 Parameter importance and partial dependence

11.5.3.1 Survival (probability of extinction end state)


Code
rf_survival_importance <- bind_rows(
  
  extract_importance(
    rf_models$survival$matri
  ) |>
    mutate(
      residence_rule = "matrilocal-matrilineal"
    ),
  
  extract_importance(
    rf_models$survival$patri
  ) |>
    mutate(
      residence_rule = "patrilocal-patrilineal"
    )
)

param_color <- parameter_metadata$color[match(rf_survival_importance$parameter, parameter_metadata$parameter)]


Note: associated colours for parameters based on their domain (general, mortality, fertility, nuptiality).

  rf_survival_importance, 
  param_color = param_color,

knitr::include_graphics(plotName)





Partial dependence plots for the top parameters influencing population survival, by residence rule.




Survival in v1.4.2 is dominated by the newly introduced labour requirement. labour_demand_per_capita is by far the strongest predictor of extinction under both residence rules, demonstrating that the ability of a population to realise environmental capacity through age-structured productive labour becomes the principal viability constraint.
density_effect_scaling_factor forms the second major control, with stronger density-dependent mortality increasing extinction probability. Fertility peak intensity (c1_fert) remains the strongest demographic counterweight: higher fertility reduces extinction risk by increasing demographic replacement.
Female union peak intensity, nominal carrying capacity, fertility and union schedule parameters, and postpartum amenorrhoea contribute at lower levels. Baseline mortality (cdmlt_level) remains relevant but is no longer one of the leading predictors.
The resulting hierarchy distinguishes v1.4.2 from the simpler demographic models. Reproduction still determines whether populations can replace losses, but survival is now primarily conditioned by the productive cost of sustaining environmental capacity and by the mortality feedback generated when that capacity becomes insufficient.
The strong importance of labour_demand_per_capita is mechanistically consistent with its role in pressure: higher labour requirements reduce effective carrying capacity, thereby increasing the demand-to-capacity ratio and exposing populations to stronger density-dependent mortality.

Partial dependence plots for the top parameters influencing population pressure, by residence rule.




labour_demand_per_capita is the strongest predictor of population pressure, particularly under patrilocal-patrilineal residence. This follows directly from the supply-side mechanism introduced in v1.4.2: increasing labour requirements reduces the share of nominal carrying capacity that a given amount of available labour can realise, thereby lowering effective carrying capacity and raising demographic pressure.
density_effect_scaling_factor remains another major control, determining how strongly a given level of pressure is translated into additional mortality. The two parameters therefore operate at different stages of the feedback: labour demand helps determine the effective capacity against which demographic demand is evaluated, while density scaling determines the demographic penalty associated with the resulting pressure.
Nominal carrying capacity, initial age structure, fertility and union schedules, and postpartum amenorrhoea provide additional variation because they affect either the environmental maximum, the demand generated by the population, or the age-specific labour available to realise that maximum.
Population pressure in v1.4.2 is thus a genuinely coupled demand-supply response. High pressure can emerge from high age-weighted consumption, restricted labour-mediated capacity, or their interaction.

Fertility peak intensity remains the strongest predictor of median age among surviving populations. Union peak intensity, fertility spread, male pre-peak union spread, and union timing provide the principal secondary controls, with several of these effects differing appreciably between residence systems.
labour_demand_per_capita has comparatively little predictive importance for median age despite dominating survival. Baseline mortality is similarly weak as a direct predictor of age composition among survivors. The labour mechanism therefore acts primarily by determining which demographic configurations remain viable and under what ecological pressure, rather than by directly reorganising age structure once persistence has been achieved.
This produces a useful division of roles: reproductive and union schedules generate demographic composition, whereas productive constraints strongly filter the set of compositions capable of surviving.

Partial dependence plots for the top parameters influencing effective carrying capacity, by residence rule.




Nominal carrying_capacity is by far the strongest predictor of effective carrying capacity under both residence systems. This follows directly from the model structure: nominal environmental capacity establishes the maximum scale that can potentially be realised, while labour availability determines what fraction of that maximum becomes effective capacity.
Fertility, union formation, mortality, and labour demand then influence effective capacity through the demographic structure that generates productive labour. Because this effective capacity forms the denominator of population pressure, variation in these mechanisms can propagate directly into the density-dependent mortality feedback.
labour_demand_per_capita therefore occupies an interesting position in the system. It strongly affects survival and pressure because it determines how difficult it is for the population to realise nominal environmental capacity, but nominal carrying_capacity remains the principal determinant of the absolute scale of effective capacity among surviving populations.

11.5.4.15 Interpretation
Age structure in v1.4.2 remains governed primarily by reproductive and union-formation processes rather than by labour demand or mortality intensity. Fertility peak intensity provides the strongest common control, while fertility timing and spread, male union timing and pre-peak union spread, and union peak intensities contribute important secondary effects.
Several fertility and female union parameters now show residence-dependent or even opposing associations, indicating that their marginal structural effects become more conditional once labour-mediated viability strongly filters the surviving population. Male union timing and pre-peak spread remain particularly influential under patrilocal-patrilineal residence.
Labour demand per capita, despite dominating extinction and population pressure, contributes relatively little directly to median age. Its principal role is therefore selective: it determines which demographic configurations remain viable much more strongly than it determines the composition of those populations once they survive.

The targeted sweep demonstrates that the effect of labour_demand_per_capita on viability is strongly nonlinear and conditional on the surrounding demographic configuration. At low and intermediate labour requirements, available labour is sufficient to keep laboured_share close to one, so effective carrying capacity remains near its nominal maximum and the resulting pressure regime changes little.
At the highest tested labour requirement under the cdmlt_level = 8 configuration, labour sufficiency begins to break down. A qualitative change appears at the highest tested value, labour_demand_per_capita = 0.60. At this level, the ensemble separates into overshooting, high-pressure persistence, and extinction outcomes, while realised labour shares decline sharply among the labour-constrained trajectories. The residence systems also begin to diverge, with the patrilocal-patrilineal ensemble showing the clearer loss of viability.
This behaviour indicates a conditional viability boundary rather than a universal threshold. Increasing labour demand has little demographic consequence while available labour remains sufficient to realise nominal capacity, but once requirements exceed the productive margin supported by a particular demographic configuration, effective capacity contracts and outcome variability increases.
To confirm that labour_demand_per_capita has such a minor effect on survival We run an additional experiment, with exactly the same configuration, except using higher Coale-Demeny level, hence lower baseline mortality.

The cdmlt_level = 14 experiment demonstrates that this transition is conditional rather than universal. With lower baseline mortality, the same labour-demand range remains compatible with full or near-full effective carrying capacity and continued viability. Labour demand therefore creates a context-dependent pressure boundary rather than a fixed collapse threshold.
This targeted result is fully compatible with the global sensitivity analysis. labour_demand_per_capita can be the strongest predictor of extinction across a heterogeneous parameter space while producing little effect within a particular favourable slice of that space. Its global importance reflects how frequently increasing labour requirements pushes already marginal demographic configurations beyond their viability boundary.

title: 11  Demand- and supply-weighted density dependent model with daily iteration (v1.4.2)
text:
11.7 Discussion notes
Version 1.4.2 completes the demand-and-supply formulation of density regulation under daily demographic scheduling. Age-weighted subsistence demand defines the demographic burden placed on the system, while age-weighted labour determines how much of the nominal environmental capacity can actually be realised. Population pressure combines these components directly as demand relative to effective carrying capacity.
The addition of productive capacity sharply restricts the viable parameter space. labour_demand_per_capita becomes the strongest predictor of extinction and population pressure, showing that viability depends critically on whether the productive structure of the population can sustain sufficient effective capacity relative to its own demographic demand.
Labour limitation nevertheless need not produce immediate collapse. Surviving populations can persist with effective carrying capacity below the nominal environmental maximum, provided the resulting demand-to-capacity ratio remains compatible with density-dependent mortality. Productive scarcity therefore operates continuously through population pressure as well as acting as a viability constraint.
The sensitivity analyses distinguish this ecological coupling from the mechanisms structuring population composition. Fertility and union formation remain the principal determinants of median age, while labour demand strongly shapes the pressure environment within which those demographic configurations can survive.
Productive limitation does not reduce all surviving populations to a single labour-sufficient state. Across the global exploration, viable populations occur with labour ratios below unity, demonstrating that partial realisation of nominal capacity can form part of a persistent regulated regime. The reference trajectory configuration occupies a more favourable region of the parameter space and maintains labour ratios above unity, illustrating that labour sufficiency and labour-constrained persistence are both possible outcomes of the same mechanism.
Internal demographic composition remains governed largely by a different set of controls. Fertility and union formation dominate median age, while labour demand and baseline mortality have comparatively weak direct effects among survivors. The supply constraint therefore acts more strongly as a filter on demographic viability than as a continuous determinant of age composition.
Residence organisation modifies several of these relationships, most clearly in male union timing and pre-peak union spread and in the association between pressure regime and median age. Yet residence differences remain conditional rather than constituting a general hierarchy of resilience.
The targeted labour-demand sweeps make the interaction explicit. A high labour requirement can strongly reduce effective capacity and trigger high pressure or extinction under one demographic configuration, while remaining compatible with full productive capacity under another. There is therefore no universal labour threshold independent of mortality, fertility, age structure, and residence organisation.
The value of v1.4.2 lies in this mechanistic separation. Simpler versions are sufficient when the research question concerns demographic replacement or unconstrained population behaviour. The full formulation becomes useful when the question specifically concerns the coupling among demographic composition, subsistence demand, productive labour, and environmentally limited capacity.
crumbs: 11  Demand- and supply-weighted density dependent model with daily iteration (v1.4.2)

title: 11  Demand- and supply-weighted density dependent model with daily iteration (v1.4.2)
text:
11.8 Chapter conclusion
Version 1.4.2 provides the most complete demand-and-supply formulation in the present model series. Population pressure now represents the ratio between age-weighted demographic demand and the carrying capacity that the population can effectively realise through its age-weighted productive labour. Nominal environmental capacity sets the potential upper limit, while demographic composition determines both the demand placed on that limit and the labour available to realise it.
The resulting sensitivity hierarchy separates the functions of these mechanisms clearly. Labour demand per capita primarily governs pressure and viability; nominal environmental capacity sets the potential scale of effective capacity; density-effect strength determines the mortality consequence of pressure; and fertility and union formation remain the principal determinants of demographic composition.
Labour limitation does not impose a universal threshold. Populations can persist under partially realised carrying capacity, while favourable demographic configurations may maintain full productive capacity even at relatively high labour requirements. Whether labour scarcity produces regulation or extinction therefore depends on its interaction with the wider demographic configuration.
Version 1.4.2 consequently does not supersede the simpler formulations for every purpose. Rather, it provides the appropriate formulation when demographic demand, productive capacity, and their reciprocal feedback with age structure are themselves part of the research question.
